strengths: Exploring the intersection between sparse autoencoders (SAEs), polysemanticity/superposition, and model steerability/safety is an exciting, timely, and conceptually interesting research direction.
The paper considers interventions across multiple granularities: SAE feature directions, token gradients, prompt injection, and individual neuron activations.
The authors conduct experiments across several models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-Instruct) and provide multiple replication plots in the appendix across random seeds.
weaknesses: Misleading terminology regarding 'black-box' interventions: The paper repeatedly claims to perform black-box interventions on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct (e.g., Abstract, Section 3.4, and Table 1). However, Section H.2 reveals that the authors 'compute gradients from and perform operations on the first half of residual layers in LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct.' Intervening in intermediate activations and calculating internal token gradients is by definition a white-box attack/intervention, not black-box.

Potential confound of syntactic priors and stopwords: In Figure 12 and Table 1, the extracted 'high-interference' tokens for locations and emotional predicates are predominantly prepositions, punctuation, and common stopwords (e.g., 'to', 'in', 'at', 'from', 'is'). In natural language, prepositions syntactically precede nouns and locations. The paper lacks controls to distinguish true polysemantic interference from simple syntactic and n-gram collocation biases.

Evaluation protocol and post-hoc filtering biases: In Appendix F.2, the authors state that they sweep the steering scale $\alpha \in [-20, 20]$ per prompt to pick the best metric outcome, and crucially, they state: 'If the similarity with the latter exceeds that with the former... we exclude such results from our statistics.' Filtering out failure cases and optimizing scale parameters per instance significantly inflates the reported intervention success and undermines the empirical claims.

Narrow evaluation limited to next-token cloze completion: The experimental setup relies entirely on synthetic cloze-style sentence fragments generated by DeepSeek-V3 to predict a single next token. The paper claims substantial safety implications ('threat surfaces', 'vulnerabilities'), yet never evaluates open-ended generation, factual accuracy across paragraphs, jailbreaks, or realistic downstream tasks.

Writing and formatting issues: There are uncompiled references (e.g., '(?)' in Appendix A.2, page 14) and broken inline figure cross-references (e.g., 'below.13' in Appendix H.3, page 25, and 'below17' in Appendix I, page 25).

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability (sparse autoencoders, superposition, polysemanticity) and model controllability/safety.
The authors explore interventions across multiple abstraction levels: feature-level steering, token gradient steering, prompt injection, and direct neuron activation editing.
The paper includes extensive supplementary experiments and replications (Figures 8–11 and 17–18) testing consistency across multiple seeds and layers.
weaknesses: Questionable framing and conceptual novelty: At the feature level, steering along an 'interfering feature' vector whose activation-space direction has high cosine similarity with a target feature will mathematically increase the projection onto that target feature by elementary linear algebra. Framing this direct geometric overlap as a surprising or distinct 'polysemantic vulnerability' is conceptually weak unless disentangled from general non-orthogonality in dense representations.

Misleading characterization of threat models: The paper repeatedly claims to demonstrate 'black-box interventions' on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct (e.g., in the abstract, Table 1, and Section 3.4). However, Section H.2 reveals that the token gradient steering actually computes gradients through and modifies the internal residual activations of the first half of LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct. Modifying internal activations is a white-box/gray-box intervention, not black-box; only the prompt prepending intervention can be considered black-box.

Potential confounds in prompt injection: In Appendix H.2 and Figure 12, the authors note that shared high-interference tokens are frequently punctuation, line breaks, or common function words (e.g., 'to', 'the', 'of', '\n'). It is unclear whether the resulting shifts in next-token distribution stem from semantic polysemantic interference or merely syntactic disruption, formatting resets, or generic sequence continuation artifacts.

Evaluation scope is limited: The evaluation relies exclusively on synthetic single-token continuation prompts generated by DeepSeek-V3, measuring only immediate top-10 next-token probability shifts. There is no assessment of actual downstream impacts, such as model utility, safety benchmarks, jailbreaks, or multi-token generation tasks.

Heuristic definitions and arbitrary thresholds: The quantification of neuron polysemanticity and 'super-neurons' relies heavily on nested heuristics (GPT-4o-mini auto-interpretation, agglomerative clustering with a relatedness threshold of 0.5, and neuron-feature connection strength thresholding at 0.2). The sensitivity of findings to these hyperparameter choices is not adequately analyzed.

Presentation and formatting defects: There are unresolved citation markers in the text (e.g., '(?)' in Section A.2 on page 14), and typos such as incomplete sentences in the introduction and abstract.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and conceptually interesting problem: understanding whether polysemanticity and representational superposition in LLMs introduce latent structural vulnerabilities that can be exploited for covert steering.
The conceptual taxonomy separating the human symbolic manifold, model activation space, and sparse feature basis provides an intuitive framing of why polysemantic interference could occur.

The authors conduct multi-level interventions (feature steering, gradient-based token steering, prompt injection, and neuron ablation/amplification), offering a broad exploratory perspective on internal representations.
weaknesses: Severe selection bias in experimental evaluation: In Appendix F.2, the authors explicitly state that if steering the interference feature causes the output to lean more toward the interference feature than the target feature, 'we exclude such results from our statistics.' Filtering out trials where the intervention failed or steered toward the unintended concept fundamentally skews the quantitative findings and invalidates the reported effect sizes.

Misuse of core terminology: The authors repeatedly claim to perform 'black-box' interventions on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct (e.g., in the Abstract, Section 3.4, Table 1, and Finding 4). However, Appendix H.2 explains that token gradient-based steering computes gradients and manipulates hidden states in the first half of residual layers. Steering internal activations and calculating model gradients is standard white-box intervention; calling it 'black-box' simply because no pre-trained SAE was available is inaccurate.

Confounded prompt and token baselines: As shown in Figure 12, the high-interference tokens identified across models are predominantly frequent functional tokens, line breaks, and common prepositions ('to', 'the', 'in', 'of', '\n'). The paper does not control for token frequency, unigram prior shifts, or syntactic position. Furthermore, the sentence completion dataset was generated by prompting DeepSeek to generate contexts where the target token naturally follows (e.g., 'After a long flight, we finally arrived in'). Without reporting the clean, unperturbed baseline accuracy for each prompt, it is impossible to disentangle how much of the target prediction is driven by the prompt context itself versus the injected interference tokens.

Per-instance metric maximization: For steering vector interventions, the scaling factor in [-20, 20] is tuned and selected to maximize improvement in the target metrics on the very sentences being evaluated (Appendix F.2). Evaluating on post-hoc optimal scale parameters per sentence without a held-out validation protocol inflates apparent intervention efficacy.

Limited evaluation scope for cross-model transfer: Cross-model transfer claims are evaluated on only two specific token categories ('locations' and 'love/hate'). Two semantic targets are insufficient to support broad claims about universal and transferable polysemantic topologies across architectures and training regimes.

Lack of controls for neuron-level analysis: The discussion of 'super-neurons' ignores well-documented architectural properties of LLMs, such as kurtosis outliers and high-norm activation channels (e.g., outlier dimensions that carry substantial residual stream norm across all contexts). Failing to control for baseline activation norms or unigram prediction biases leaves the interpretation of these neurons unsupported.

strengths: Novel and intriguing research question investigating whether polysemantic interference structures in LLM activation spaces are stochastic artifacts or reflect transferable representational geometry across model scales and families.

Comprehensive multi-locus intervention framework that systematically compares interventions across four distinct levels: sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature directions, token gradients, prompt injection, and individual neuron activations.
Broad experimental scope spanning small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) with pre-trained SAEs to black-box instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-Instruct).

Thorough supplementary material documenting distribution statistics, sensitivity to clustering cutoffs, alternative metrics (weighted overlap), and comparisons between different auto-interpretation models (GPT-4o-mini vs. DeepSeek-V3).
weaknesses: The claims regarding cross-model transferability are significantly stronger than what the empirical evidence supports. In Table 1 and Table 5, out of eight evaluated semantic categories, five fail to demonstrate generalizability (Table 5). Even among the three selected 'strong' categories (Table 1), the effect size in prompt injection on larger models is often marginal (e.g., Gemma-2-9B on Science shows 20.40% for high-interference vs. 20.15% for random; Gemma-2-9B on Locations is only ~2% above random).

Potential confounding factors in the neuron-level analysis: Highly polysemantic neurons / 'super-neurons' (Section 3.6) typically exhibit higher firing frequency and larger activation magnitudes. The observation that amplifying them causes larger output shifts may simply reflect basic activation norm/energy properties rather than polysemantic architecture specifically; the study lacks controls for base neuron activation magnitude or frequency.

Questionable model attribution and reproducibility concerns regarding model names: The paper repeatedly cites using 'GPT-5-mini' for post-hoc annotations and paired comparisons (Section 3.5, Appendix C, Appendix M). As no publicly available or documented model exists under this designation, this creates confusion and undermines experimental reproducibility.

Incomplete text and drafting errors: Several sentences end abruptly or contain obvious missing placeholders, such as the final sentence of the Abstract ('Code and data are available' with no period or link), Appendix O ('This paper follows the This study has three key methodological limitations.'), and Appendix P ('...synthetic data in but deliberately omit...').

Limited evaluation on realistic downstream tasks: Most evaluations rely on synthetic next-token prediction prompts generated by LLMs. The brief test on HellaSwag in Appendix L is small-scale (500 samples) and largely anecdotal, leaving open the question of whether these interventions produce meaningful behavioral control beyond local next-token distribution distortion.

strengths: Investigates an intriguing and important question in mechanistic interpretability: whether interference patterns between polysemantic features are systematic and whether they can transfer across models.
Proposes a multi-level intervention framework examining feature directions, token gradients, prompt injection, and individual neurons.
The paper is ambitious in scope, testing hypotheses across multiple model families and sizes (Pythia, GPT-2, Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
weaknesses: Triviality of the core linear algebra mechanism: In Section 3.1, the authors define 'interference' between two SAE features fi and fj as the cosine similarity between their decoder directions in the model's activation space A_l. Showing that steering along fi shifts predictions in the direction of fj when cos(w_i, w_j) is large (>0.4) is mathematically expected; adding a vector w_i to activations naturally adds a significant positive projection along w_j. Framing this as a surprising finding about polysemantic vulnerability overstates an elementary property of non-orthogonal vectors.

Substantial cherry-picking in cross-model transfer claims: The main text (Section 3.3 and Table 1) claims that polysemantic interference patterns 'transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models' based on three selected categories (Locations, Number, Science). However, Appendix Table 5 reveals that five out of eight evaluated categories (Person, Animal, Emotion, Color, Time) exhibit no strong generalizability, with high-interference tokens often performing worse than or indistinguishable from a random baseline. This severely undercuts the central claim of universal transferability.

Marginal effect sizes in black-box prompt injection: In Table 1, the difference in success rate between high-interference tokens and the random baseline is often only 1 to 3 percentage points (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B locations: 20.78% vs. 18.24%; Gemma-2-9B locations: 12.71% vs. 10.66%). Given that success is defined merely as elevating target tokens into the top-30 predictions, these shifts are practically negligible and likely subject to minor token-frequency or context confounding.

Questionable experimental details and unverifiable models: In Section 3.5, Appendix C, and Appendix M, the authors repeatedly refer to evaluations conducted with 'GPT-5-mini' (alongside DeepSeek-V3). Since 'GPT-5-mini' is not an existing public model, this raises serious concerns regarding reproducibility, provenance of the evaluation, or unverified naming.

Speculative post-hoc storytelling: The analysis of counterintuitive shared structures relies heavily on LLM-generated rationalizations and post-hoc justifications (such as hypothesizing a latent biographical link between 'Beethoven' and 'frustration/annoyance' due to his deafness). Such unfalsifiable interpretations do not constitute rigorous evidence for latent knowledge organization.

Incomplete text and draft quality issues: The manuscript contains multiple glaring omissions, such as incomplete sentences in Appendix O ('This paper follows the This study has three key methodological limitations.') and incomplete links in Appendix P ('and synthetic data in but deliberately omit...').

strengths: Interesting conceptual premise connecting mechanistic interpretability (specifically sparse autoencoders and superposition) to cross-model behavioral control and adversarial vulnerabilities.
Comprehensive multi-locus intervention framework evaluating interventions across four distinct levels: feature directions, token gradients, prompt injection, and individual neurons.

Attempts cross-model and cross-scale evaluation, testing whether interference patterns discovered in small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) can transfer to steer large instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B, Gemma-2-9B).
weaknesses: Overstated generalizability claims: The main text highlights three categories (Location, Number, Science) showing positive prompt-injection transfer, but Appendix Table 5 reveals that five out of the eight tested categories (Person, Animal, Emotion, Color, Time) do not demonstrate strong generalizability. This indicates that the phenomenon may not be universal or robust across general semantic domains.

Tautological aspects of the core geometric finding: 'Interference' is defined as the cosine similarity between SAE feature vectors in activation space. Intervening along one vector naturally shifts activations along any collinear or non-orthogonal vector by simple vector arithmetic; thus, behavioral shifts between interfering features are largely an expected consequence of linear algebra rather than an emergent property of polysemanticity.

Reliance on noisy semantic definitions: Semantic dissimilarity is determined using embeddings of auto-generated feature glosses (via GPT-4o-mini / text-embedding-3-large). The low inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa of 0.22–0.41 between DeepSeek-V3 and GPT-5-mini) highlights that what the metric classifies as 'semantically unrelated' frequently contains latent co-occurrence, syntactic, or contextual relatedness.

Optimization bias in intervention evaluation: As noted in Section H.2, the intervention scale parameter is tuned across [-20, 20] on the test sentences and the maximum improvement is recorded, introducing substantial optimization bias into the reported metrics.

Incomplete text and editorial issues: Several sentences cut off or contain missing placeholders (e.g., end of Abstract: 'Code and data are available'; Appendix O: 'This paper follows the This study has three key methodological limitations.'; Appendix P: 'synthetic data in but deliberately omit...').
